meta.title: Destination Image, Perceived Medical Service Quality and Revisit Intention among International Medical Tourists: Evidence from Eastern India

synthesis.executive_assessment:
The manuscript addresses a relevant question — how destination image and perceived medical service quality shape revisit intention among international medical tourists — in an under-studied regional context. The model is theoretically plausible, the sample is reasonably large, and the PLS-SEM analysis is reported in more detail than is typical for the field.

However, in its current form the paper would face substantial resistance at Tourism Management. The research gap is framed mainly as a contextual gap ("no study in Eastern India") without explaining why this context should change theory. Causal language repeatedly exceeds a single-source, cross-sectional design; common method bias is addressed only with Harman's single-factor test; and the sample size reported in the abstract (n = 430) differs from the usable sample in the methods (n = 412). The multigroup comparison between domestic and international patients is reported without MICOM invariance testing.

None of these issues is fatal. With a sharper theoretical contribution, corrected reporting and additional robustness analyses, the study could be competitive.
synthesis.readiness_rationale: Six major issues — mainly the contribution framing, causal overclaiming, CMB treatment and missing measurement invariance — would likely lead to a major-revision or desk-reject decision at a Q1 tourism journal. All are fixable before submission.

desk_rejection_risks.why: Tourism Management editors routinely desk-reject 'new country' replications without theoretical advancement.
desk_rejection_risks.fix: Reframe the gap around a boundary condition of signalling / cue-utilisation theory that medical travel uniquely tests.

desk_rejection_risks.risk: Causal claims from cross-sectional survey data
desk_rejection_risks.why: Reviewers will question every 'drives' and 'leads to' statement.
desk_rejection_risks.fix: Replace with associational language and add an explicit causal-inference limitation.

journal_fit.notes: Topic fits the journal's scope on tourist behaviour, but the managerial framing is stronger than the theoretical one that TM expects.

dimension_ratings.evidence: Signalling theory is named but not used to derive H3–H5 (A04).
Good coverage; 22% of references from the last five years.
Purposive hospital-based sampling; limited non-response checks (A06).
Validated scales, loadings > .70, AVE and CR above thresholds.
H4 described as supported despite a non-significant path (A07).
Findings compared with prior studies but mechanisms under-explained.
Questionnaire provided; no data availability statement.
Several STROBE items missing (response rate, bias).

major_strengths: Clear and policy-relevant research problem for a fast-growing medical tourism corridor.
Well-established measurement scales with strong reliability and convergent validity.
Transparent PLS-SEM reporting including HTMT, bootstrapped CIs and PLSpredict.
major_concerns: The gap is framed as contextual rather than theoretical.
Causal language exceeds a single-source cross-sectional design.
Common method bias is assessed only with Harman's test.
H4 interpreted as supported although the path is not significant.

major_comments.heading: Sharpen the theoretical contribution
major_comments.comment: The introduction argues that the study is novel because no prior work has examined these relationships among medical tourists in Eastern India. A Q1 reviewer will ask why this context matters theoretically. Medical travel involves high-stakes credence services; this is an opportunity to show how destination image acts as a signal under extreme information asymmetry — a boundary condition that ordinary leisure-tourism studies cannot test.
major_comments.evidence: [[PAGE 3]] "To the best of our knowledge, no study has examined these relationships among medical tourists in Eastern India."
major_comments.author_action: Rewrite the gap paragraph around signalling/cue-utilisation theory and state one or two explicit theoretical contributions.

major_comments.heading: Temper causal claims
major_comments.comment: The discussion states that service quality 'drives' revisit intention and that destination image 'leads to' trust. With single-source cross-sectional data these are associations.
major_comments.evidence: [[PAGE 21]] "perceived medical service quality drives revisit intention more strongly than destination image"
major_comments.author_action: Replace causal verbs; add a limitation on causal inference and suggest longitudinal or experimental follow-ups.

major_comments.heading: Establish measurement invariance before the multigroup comparison
major_comments.comment: Group differences between first-time and repeat medical tourists are interpreted without MICOM, so observed differences may reflect measurement non-equivalence.
major_comments.evidence: [[PAGE 18]] "A multigroup analysis was performed to compare first-time and repeat visitors."
major_comments.author_action: Run and report the three-step MICOM procedure before PLS-MGA.

major_comments.heading: Common method bias needs stronger treatment
major_comments.comment: Harman's single-factor test is insufficient on its own for same-source, same-time data.
major_comments.evidence: [[PAGE 14]] "Harman's single-factor test showed that a single factor explained 31.2% of the variance"
major_comments.author_action: Add procedural remedies taken at data collection and a full-collinearity VIF or marker-variable test.

minor_comments.comment: Report p-values below .001 as p < .001 rather than p = .000.
The response rate and number of refusals are not reported.
minor_comments.author_action: Add to the sampling section (STROBE item 13).

minor_comments.comment: Four references lack DOIs that are available in Crossref.
The conceptual model figure labels the mediator 'Trust' while the text uses 'Destination trust'.

comments: Open with the theoretical puzzle, not market-size statistics.
Justify hospital-based purposive sampling and discuss selection bias.
Report data collection dates consistently (methods say 2025, discussion says 2024).
Explain the non-significant H4 rather than reframing it.

assessments.methodological: Adequate cross-sectional design with purposive sampling in three hospitals; selection and non-response bias need discussion.
assessments.statistical: PLS-SEM is appropriately reported (HTMT, bootstrap CIs, PLSpredict); MGA lacks invariance testing and CMB testing is weak.
assessments.theoretical: Signalling theory is invoked but not used to derive hypotheses.
assessments.contribution: Currently contextual and managerial; needs a clear theoretical increment.
assessments.reproducibility: Items and analysis settings are reported; a data availability statement is missing.

editor_only_concerns: Whether the contribution goes beyond a regional replication of well-established relationships.
Reviewer availability may be limited for medical-tourism studies from this region, so the framing must stand on its own.

priority_1_must_fix.action: Reconcile the sample size (430 vs 412) across abstract, methods and tables.
Re-interpret H4 as not supported and discuss why.

priority_2_substantive.action: Reframe the research gap and contribution theoretically.
Run MICOM before the multigroup analysis.
Add full-collinearity VIF or marker-variable CMB test.
Replace causal language and add a causal-inference limitation.

priority_3_strengthening.action: Discuss selection and non-response bias of hospital-based sampling.

priority_4_editorial.action: Correct p = .000 reporting and add missing DOIs.
Harmonise construct labels between text and Figure 1.

synthesis.reviewer_letter:
Summary
The authors examine how destination image and perceived medical service quality relate to trust and revisit intention among 412 international medical tourists in Eastern India, using PLS-SEM.

Overall assessment
The topic is relevant and the measurement is strong. My main concerns relate to the theoretical contribution, causal interpretation, common method bias, and the multigroup analysis.

Major comments
1. The research gap is contextual. Please explain what this context adds to theory...
2. Causal language (e.g., 'drives', 'leads to') is not supported by a cross-sectional design...
3. Please establish measurement invariance (MICOM) before comparing groups...
4. Harman's single-factor test alone does not rule out common method bias...

Minor comments
1. Report p < .001 instead of p = .000.
2. Report the response rate.
3. Harmonise construct labels.

Recommendation (for the author's planning): major revision before submission.
cover_letter_tips: Lead with the theoretical contribution, not the regional context.
Disclose the conference version presented at the 2025 regional tourism conference, if applicable.
synthesis.limitations_of_this_review: This review is based on the manuscript text only; statistics were checked for internal consistency but not recomputed from raw data. Novelty was not verified against a full literature database.

style_review.overall_note: Most of the manuscript is specific to its context, but the introduction and implications sections contain generic phrasing that editors may read as template text, and no AI-use disclosure statement was found.
style_review.style_shift_note: The introduction reads noticeably more generic and polished than the methods and results sections.
style_review.disclosure_advice: Check the target journal's generative-AI policy and add a disclosure statement (or a statement that no AI tools were used) before the references.

passages.quote: In today's rapidly evolving landscape, medical tourism plays a pivotal role in shaping the multifaceted dynamics of healthcare economies.
passages.why_it_matters: Opening sentences like this give the editor no information about the study and are common in unedited AI output.
passages.suggestion: Open with a concrete figure, e.g. the number of international patients treated in Odisha in 2024, with a citation.

passages.quote: These findings offer valuable insights for policymakers, practitioners and scholars alike.
passages.why_it_matters: The implication could fit any study.
passages.suggestion: Name the specific decision a hospital marketing manager or the state tourism department could change based on the H2 result.

caveats: The free overlap screen checks a sample of sentences against open-access full texts, titles and abstracts (OpenAlex, Europe PMC). It cannot see paywalled articles, theses, student papers or most web pages, so a clean result does NOT mean the manuscript will pass Turnitin/iThenticate.
Run a full similarity check (iThenticate/Turnitin, or DrillBit through your university library under INFLIBNET ShodhShuddhi) before submission; journals use iThenticate (Crossref Similarity Check).

The writing-authenticity review flags wording that editors may read as generic or template-like. It does not detect or prove AI use, and no score is given because AI detectors produce false positives - especially for non-native English writing and formulaic methods sections.
Follow the target journal's policy on generative-AI use and include a disclosure statement when AI tools were used for writing or editing.
